History:
• 45-year-old female housekeeper presents with painful, dry, cracked skin of both palms, onset 3–4 months ago after starting a new hotel housekeeping job.  
• Gradual progression; pain and itching now severe enough to miss work for the past 3 days.  
• Intermittent pruritus; occasional bleeding only after scratching.  
• Mild generalized dryness on legs, long-standing, not bothersome.  
• Denies fever, nausea, vomiting, bowel or urinary changes. Appetite and general wellbeing normal.  
• Occupational exposure to cleaning chemicals; inconsistent glove use.  
• Self-treatment: OTC E45 emollient (no benefit) and an unspecified antihistamine (no benefit).

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• No prior skin disease (eczema/dermatitis) reported.  
• Medications: Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented; OTC E45 cream; antihistamine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: No known drug or environmental allergies.  
• Family history: Diabetes; no known dermatologic diseases.  
• Social: Non-smoker; alcohol “a couple of pints per week.”

Physical Examination:
• Patient-reported: Dry, fissured, erythematous skin on palms with occasional bleeding when scratched; tenderness and pruritus present.  
• No systemic symptoms reported.  
• Alert and oriented via teleconsultation.  
• Additional vitals or in-person exam findings not documented.

Impression:
• Occupational irritant/contact dermatitis of the hands.

Management Plan:
• Avoidance: Wear protective gloves at all times when using cleaning products.  
• Pharmacologic: Prescription for topical corticosteroid cream (potency and regimen not documented) plus stronger emollient; instructed to apply emollient liberally 3–4×/day for 2 weeks.  
• Monitoring: If no improvement or worsening within 10–14 days, return for reassessment sooner; otherwise routine follow-up in 2 weeks.  
• Prescription sent electronically to patient’s pharmacy.

Patient Summary:
Ms Parkinson likely has contact dermatitis from repeated chemical exposure as a hotel housekeeper. She has been started on topical steroid therapy and frequent emollient use, with strict advice to wear gloves.

Key Takeaways:
• Always wear gloves when cleaning to prevent further skin irritation.  
• Apply the prescribed steroid cream and thick emollient 3–4 times daily for the next 2 weeks.  
• Seek review earlier if cracking, pain, or spread worsens, or if no improvement in 10–14 days.

Next Steps:
• Begin prescribed topical treatments today.  
• Follow-up appointment/televisit in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms persist or worsen.  
• Consider dermatology referral or patch testing if inadequate response (to be decided at follow-up).

Quality checks:
• Missing data: No vital signs; no objective skin examination findings documented; steroid potency/dosing unspecified; full medication reconciliation limited.  
• No internal transcript conflicts noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio; minor conversational fillers but overall good.
